reason: The run renders one sense five ways: affliction (most chapters), suffering (Matthew 24), distress (Mark 13, John 16:33, Philippians 1:17, James 1:27), trouble (Mark 4:17, Acts 11:19) and hardship (Acts 14:22). Parallel passages diverge: Matthew 13:21 'affliction' against Mark 4:17 'trouble'; Matthew 24:21, 29 'suffering' against Mark 13:19, 24 'distress'; and the 'great θλῖψις' is 'great suffering' in Matthew 24:21 but 'great affliction' in Revelation 7:14. The departure from 'tribulation' is made everywhere, but onto different words, so readers cannot see that the same term recurs.
sense: Pressure in the figurative sense: hardship, oppression or trouble that bears down on a person or people, usually from outside circumstances or hostile parties. This includes the end-time passages (Matthew 24, Mark 13, Revelation 7:14).

alternates.when: Only where the word names inward or bodily anguish rather than hardship imposed by circumstances or opponents: the woman's pain in childbirth (John 16:21) and Paul's anguish of heart when writing (2 Corinthians 2:4). Do not use 'distress' where στενοχωρία or ἀνάγκη stands alongside and needs that word (Romans 2:9; 8:35; 1 Thessalonians 3:7).

rationale: In the period, including the Septuagint, θλῖψις was an ordinary word for oppressive hardship, not a technical term. 'Tribulation' is now heard by many readers as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. 'Affliction' is an established traditional rendering alongside it (the King James Version uses both), carries the idea of hardship pressing on someone, and is already the run's majority choice. Using it in the Gospels, Paul and Revelation alike lets the reader see the same word in 'great affliction' at Matthew 24:21, Acts 7:11 and Revelation 7:14, and it leaves 'distress' free for στενοχωρία and ἀνάγκη when they are paired with it.
standard_view: Lexicons agree on the sense: oppression, affliction, distress, with an occasional inward sense of anguish. English versions split. KJV and ESV alternate between 'tribulation' and 'affliction'; NRSV often has 'suffering', 'affliction', 'distress' or 'ordeal'; NIV uses 'trouble', 'distress', 'suffering', 'hardships' and 'persecution' (Acts 11:19), keeping 'tribulation' only at Revelation 7:14. Many versions retain 'great tribulation' in Matthew 24:21 and Revelation 7:14. Whether Revelation 7:14 refers to a single final crisis or to the whole course of the church's suffering is debated, but that is a question of reference, not of the word's meaning.
